Presidents, prices at the pump, and the difference in perceptions between energy market experts and non-experts
abstract: We conduct a survey of US-based energy market experts and non-experts and find that non-experts are significantly more likely to believe the US President plays a major role in determining retail fuel prices. Next, we analyze weekly retail gasoline and diesel price data from the US, UK, France, and Canada under different heads of state. After controlling for fluctuations in the wholesale crude oil price, country-specific long-run averages in prices, common time shocks, and national fuel excise taxes, we find that fuel prices differ significantly across leaders. Although we do not claim to have established a causal link between executive regime change and retail fuel price variation, our fuel price analysis does help explain why many people believe political executives can influence retail gasoline prices. We also make a call to economists to fill the notable gap in the economic and policy research on the influence of executive action on retail fuel prices and to look for other potential gaps by paying closer attention to similarly prominent economic narratives.

title: Macroeconomic risk, political instability, and environmental sustainability risk: assessing vulnerabilities among emerging and developing economies
Designing renewable energy auctions for high realization probability — CfD and payment-only auctions
abstract: In recent years, different instruments for renewable energy expansion have been debated. Among support and hedging instruments, two-sided contracts for difference (CfDs) have become the default in many countries and are promoted by the European Commission. At the same time, payment-only auctions (e.g., seabed lease auction for offshore wind) have also become established, where the electricity sales are unregulated, but winners pay for the right to build and operate energy plants. Considering both cost uncertainty in the form of post-auction shocks and revenue uncertainty, we compare two-sided CfDs with payment-only auctions. Contrary to conventional wisdom, the non-realization risk is higher with auctioned CfDs than with payment-only auctions and is exacerbated by risk aversion, when developers can cope with both options. This result is reinforced when payments are due before the implementation decision. It can be altered in either direction by information updates about the future electricity market during the implementation period. Auctioneer’s expected costs are higher in payment-only auctions if the bidders are risk-averse or risk-neutral and have higher costs. Thus, there is a trade-off for the auctioneer between realization and revenue. CfDs are particularly useful when developers need support or hedging for project implementation. Against this backdrop and considering asymmetric information, i.e., developers know best the economic conditions of their projects, we propose a design in which developers decide competitively between a CfD auction and a payment-only auction and which enhances the realization probability.

title: Fuel taxes without borders: Tax-induced price changes and recorded fuel sales in the European Union
abstract: This paper estimates how retail fuel prices and cross-border price differentials affect recorded domestic road-fuel sales in the European Union, using harmonized monthly panel data for 24 countries from January 2008 through December 2025. We use tax-induced variation in retail prices, instrumenting domestic prices and relative price gaps with statutory fuel-tax variables in two-stage least squares models with country and month fixed effects. We complement the country-month analysis with directed dyadic IV specifications that compare home and neighbouring countries within land-border pairs. The outcome is recorded domestic fuel sales, not physical fuel consumption within national borders, so the estimates capture both changes in fuel use and shifts in the location where purchases are recorded. For diesel, the preferred country-month IV estimate implies an own-price elasticity of approximately −1.40 for recorded domestic road-diesel sales. For gasoline, the preferred estimate is also negative, approximately −0.78, although it is less stable across demanding sensitivity specifications. The clearest evidence of cross-border reallocation comes from the dyadic IV design. When the dyadic price differential is defined as the neighbour's log price minus the home country's log price, the cross-border coefficient is positive and close to +0.53 for both diesel and gasoline. This means that recorded domestic sales increase when neighbouring countries become more expensive relative to the home country. The findings imply that uncoordinated national fuel-tax changes can shift where purchases are recorded, potentially eroding domestic tax bases and complicating the interpretation of national fuel-sales statistics in integrated markets.

Financing the low-carbon transition: Do energy transition investments improve ESG performance?
abstract: Energy transition investment ( eti ) has emerged as a central component of global climate finance, yet its firm-level consequences remain insufficiently understood. Using BloombergNEF energy-transition investment data and Refinitiv ESG measures, we examine whether aggregate transition-finance deployment influences corporate sustainability performance. We find that higher eti exposure is associated with significant improvements in environmental, social, and governance ( esg ) performance, with the strongest gains observed in the environmental pillar. The positive association is stronger among firms with greater climate-related innovative capacity and among low-carbon firms, whereas esg gains are comparatively smaller in high-carbon sectors despite the economic importance of eti for managing transition risk. Robustness analyses based on dynamic System Generalized Method of Moments (SGMM) estimation, external instrumental-variable techniques, and Granger-causality tests indicate that eti precedes and predicts subsequent esg improvements. Overall, the findings identify a macro-to-micro transmission mechanism through which large-scale transition-finance deployment shapes firm behavior and sustainability outcomes, establishing eti as an important driver of multidimensional corporate sustainability performance.

Trading electrons: Predicting DART spread spikes in ISO electricity markets
abstract: We study the problem of forecasting and optimally trading day-ahead versus realtime (DART) price spreads in U.S. wholesale electricity markets. Building on the framework of [9], we extend spike prediction from a single zone to a multi-zone setting and treat both positive and negative DART spikes within a unified statistical model. To translate directional signals into economically meaningful positions, we develop a structural and market-consistent price impact model based on day-ahead bid stacks. This yields closed-form expressions for the optimal vector of zonal INC/DEC quantities, capturing asymmetric buy/sell impacts and cross-zone congestion effects. When applied to NYISO, the resulting impact-aware strategy significantly improves the risk-return profile relative to unit-size trading and highlights substantial heterogeneity across markets and seasons.

abstract: This paper introduces a new approach for bubble detection based on mixed causal and noncausal autoregressive processes and their tail process representation during an explosive episode. Departing from traditional definitions of bubbles as nonstationary and temporarily explosive processes, we adopt a perspective in which prices are assumed to follow a strictly stationary process, with the bubble considered an intrinsic component of its nonlinear dynamics. The proposed approach provides a bubble indicator for detecting bubbles and measuring their duration. We implement our strategy to investigate the phenomenon called the "green bubble" in the field of renewable energy investment.

Isolated or interconnected? An equilibrium framework for swarm electrification in rural energy planning
abstract: Swarm electrification–the interconnection of isolated decentralized energy systems for local energy sharing– could accelerate rural electrification, yet it remains largely absent from major initiatives that still prioritize solar home systems and centralized mini-grids. To determine when swarm interconnection is most justified, we develop a techno-economic decision-support framework, introducing three heterogeneity indexes: budget heterogeneity (BHI), demand shape diversity (SDI), and demand peak diversity (PDI). We use these indexes to investigate how heterogeneity increases the value of interconnection in the swarm-grid setting. We translate model outputs into policy-relevant indicators, e.g., avoided investment and added social welfare, and combine these into a single benefit ratio (BR). Using mixed complementarity problem (MCP) models–common in market and other equilibrium settings–we simulate decentralized energy trading under two competitive assumptions: perfect competition and Cournot competition, thus deriving tariff levels endogenously. We also include a central-planning benchmark where prices are exogenously fixed. Results from a Madagascar case study indicate that heterogeneity reshapes the economic rationale for interconnection. Demand differences yield at least 3% avoided investment through more efficient allocation and reduced oversizing, and complementary load-profiles increase energy sharing more than fivefold. Budget heterogeneity dominates, inducing over fifteen times more energy sharing by redistributing investments across nanogrids. Different market designs highlight a profitability-affordability trade-off: payback periods as short as 1.5 years are maximized under cost-recovery-oriented settings, imposing higher tariffs and underscoring the need for governance mechanisms aligned with energy-justice objectives. This framework offers practical guidance for a more adaptive and socially-inclusive rural electrification.

title: Shock amplification and delayed recovery in resource economies: The role of fiscal policy reform
abstract: This paper examines how global commodity price shocks propagate through resource-dependent economies, with a focus on the interaction between extraction costs and domestic policy responses. We develop a simple framework in which high-cost producers are more exposed to negative price shocks, but the persistence of their response depends on investment conditions and policy environments. We test these predictions using the 2014–2016 oil price collapse, comparing Alberta—one of the world’s highest-cost oil producers—to a synthetic control constructed from lower-cost jurisdictions. Alberta experienced significantly larger declines in hydrocarbon output, investment, and per capita GDP, along with a more prolonged recovery. However, placebo analyses for other high-cost jurisdictions reveal no comparable declines, indicating that cost structure alone is insufficient to explain the observed contraction. Exploiting within-province variation, we further show that Alberta’s response to the 2015 shock differs markedly from its response to the 2009 collapse, despite an unchanged cost structure. Event-study estimates indicate that the post-2015 decline is closely associated with contemporaneous fiscal policy changes. While policy responses may be endogenous, the combined evidence points to a transmission mechanism in which domestic policy shapes—and potentially amplifies—the effects of external shocks in high-cost environments.

abstract: Russia’s weaponization of gas supplies has heightened concerns over the energy trilemma—security, affordability, and sustainability—emphasizing the need to reduce dependence on volatile fossil fuel markets. This paper investigates speculative price dynamics in energy markets during the recent energy crisis, focusing on gas, electricity, low-carbon hydrogen, and renewable Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs). We apply the Phillips, Shi, and Yu (2015) mild explosivity (PSY) test to daily and weekly benchmark price series to detect and date-stamp bubble episodes. Our analysis identifies two significant periods of widespread exuberance: one beginning in mid-2021 and another peaking in August 2022, coinciding with the Nord Stream I pipeline shutdown. These results provide empirical evidence of boom-and-bust cycles driven by both geopolitical supply shocks and market speculation. The findings stress the structural fragility of fossil-based energy systems and reinforce the urgency of accelerating the transition toward more stable, low-carbon energy alternatives.

abstract: The aim of this paper is to determine from market expectations how firms are affected by environmental regulatory risk. We use a text-based measure of environmental regulatory stringency derived from US EPA legal documents and industry-level relevance scores to capture time-varying regulatory risk exposure. We find that environmental regulatory stringency carries a positive and statistically significant risk premium, especially for firms with high cash holdings. For firms with low cash holdings, the effect is highly volatile, showing investors are uncertain about a firms future when faced with stricter regulation. Firms' environmental profiles further matter, as high-emission firms returns are negatively affected when regulatory stringency increases. Because regulatory text is released infrequently, challenging real-time risk analysis, we utilise our studies insights to derive a highfrequency, market-expectation capturing Environmental Regulatory Risk Index (ERRI). We show that ERRI captures shifts in investors' expectations of environmental regulatory risk and how it reacts during environmental policy and political developments, thereby providing a high-frequency measure to evaluate and compare environmental regulatory risk.

title: Carbon-price-equivalent signals in multilateral energy reforms: Evidence from developing and transition economies
Day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme via stochastic robust optimization
abstract: The high integration of renewable energy technologies in power systems represents a challenge due to the uncertainty in their production. In most European markets, producers should comply with their scheduled operation or face the penalties imposed through an imbalance mechanism. Renewable energy sources can be coordinated along with other technologies within a virtual power plant to mitigate the imbalance penalties. To mitigate this issue, in this paper a day-ahead market scheduling strategy of a virtual power plant under the single imbalance pricing scheme is determined using a novel two-stage formulation. The first stage comprises the day-ahead market scheduling, while the second stage involves rescheduling of the assets once the deviations in the renewable production availability, modeled using scenarios, are known. Novelty of this work lies in the combination of scenario-based stochastic programming and robust optimization to model uncertainty in the imbalance price deviations. The risk of the decision maker is controlled using the conditional value-at-risk for a given confidence level. The presented case study is based on data from the Croatian power system. Numerical results demonstrate that the proposed formulation outperforms the formulation of previous works in reducing the arbitrage between the day-ahead market and the imbalance settlement. Moreover, in-sample and out-of-sample simulations lead to similar profits. Furthermore, the benefits of changing the risk-aversion level of the decision maker at the different stages of the problem are evaluated.

Critical peak pricing or rebate? An impact analysis in a cold climate market
abstract: As electricity becomes more important to meet the energy needs of societies, electricity demand management is increasingly being used. Dynamic pricing, in particular, can contribute to lower consumption during peak periods. Critical peak pricing (CPP) and critical peak rebate (CPR) can be used to specifically target potentially problematic periods and reduce load. Using a very large set of data (15-minute consumption of 13,504 consumers over three winters) and a difference-in-difference (DID) approach, we show that CPP consumers achieve larger reductions than CPR consumers, and that the extent of the reduction in both cases decreases over time. We also find that CPP consumers do not shift their load and larger CPP consumers significantly reduce their consumption in non-critical peak periods. Analyzing subgroups of consumers with different average consumption levels, we also find that the size of the reduction to be heterogeneous across groups. Finally, because CPR requires a reference consumption level, compensated reductions may exceed the causal reductions estimated from the DID analysis, raising potential concerns about the cost-effectiveness and distributional implications of baseline-based rebate programs.

Negative electricity prices and strategic energy storage resources with high renewable penetration
abstract: Negative electricity prices are becoming increasingly frequent in electricity markets due to incentive-driven bidding behaviors associated with renewable support schemes. This paper investigates the impact of price-making energy storage resources on market outcomes in the presence of renewable production incentives. We develop a bi-level model to examine three dimensions of strategic storage behavior: system costs and storage profits, electricity prices, and supplier surplus across generators. The upper level represents a storage profit maximization model, and the lower level represents the market operator’s economic dispatch problem. Using the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) system in the U.S. as a case study, we find that strategic storage behaviors increase storage arbitrage profits by 22%–126%, while raising system generation cost by less than 1% relative to a centrally controlled storage benchmark, when storage power capacity equals 14% of peak demand. In addition, negative electricity prices become more frequent due to storage’s capacity withholding mechanisms. Fossil-fueled generators experience surplus gains of up to 3% under strategic storage at high renewable penetration levels with negative price conditions. Future wholesale market designs should explicitly incorporate renewable policy incentive design and strategic storage behaviors, particularly given their joint effects on negative price formation and welfare distribution.

Long-term impacts of climate change on electricity demand and household expenditure in Saudi Arabia
abstract: With regional warming across the Arabian Peninsula occurring at twice the global average and driving summer peak electricity loads to nearly 80% of total system capacity, understanding long-term energy implications is critical for Saudi Arabia’s national climate resilience. Consequently, this study assesses the impacts of climate change on thermal comfort, energy demand, and household electricity expenditure through 2100. Using the multi-sectoral Global Change Assessment Model for the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (GCAM-KSA), we integrated three regionally updated Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP1-3) with two climate pathways: RCP7.0 (high impact) and RCP2.6 (low impact). Our results indicate a shift in thermal conditions by 2100 relative to the 1981–2014 baseline. Cooling Degree Days (CDD) are projected to increase up to 24% and 80% under the low and high-impact pathways, respectively, while Heating Degree Days (HDD) remain negligible. Furthermore, the temporal distribution of CDD expands significantly, representing a substantial lengthening of the summer season beyond mid-century. By isolating socioeconomic and climate drivers, we find that high socioeconomic development (SSP3) initially drives a 33–53% rise in cooling demand through 2060 compared to 2025. However, climate impacts emerge as the dominant accelerator between 2060 and 2100, independently driving cooling service demand up by an additional 38–49% (RCP7.0) and 13–16% (RCP2.6). Consequently, annual average household expenditures attributable to climate impacts are projected to increase by 32–45% (RCP7.0) and 7–11% (RCP2.6) in 2100. These findings highlight the importance of integrating climate adaptation strategies into long-term energy planning to mitigate rising household expenditure.

title: Effects of trade barriers on foreign direct investment: Evidence from Chinese solar panels
abstract: Trade barriers can affect firms’ international investment decisions, not only the trade flows they directly target. This paper studies the anti-dumping and countervailing duties (AD-CVDs) imposed by the United States in 2012 on Chinese solar panel imports and examines how affected Chinese firms adjusted their foreign direct investment decisions. Due to their differential exposure to U.S. trade policy, Chinese firms are granted different AD-CVD rates. I leverage this variation to develop a difference-in-differences design. Using monthly greenfield FDI announcement data from 2009 to 2018 and a Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood estimator, I find that targeted firms increased FDI by 145 million dollars in 2012, relative to a pre-policy average of 9 million dollars. The effects are larger and more persistent among firms already active in FDI before the policy. The greenfield FDI response does not carry over to cross-border mergers and acquisitions. Location choice analysis suggests that targeted firms shifted investment toward Asia, especially after a second round of AD-CVD measures in 2015. Descriptive trade and investment data provide suggestive evidence consistent with production relocation and export-platform FDI. These results document FDI diversion that modifies investment patterns in the short run and is consistent with trade-barrier avoidance in the medium run.

Do crises integrate or fragment energy transition metals markets? Evidence from a connectedness-based crisis typology
abstract: This paper develops a two-dimensional crisis typology that classifies the impact of major crisis episodes on return spillover connectedness across energy transition metals (ETM) markets. Using daily data for 17 metals, spanning base metals, precious metals, battery metals, and technology metals, and the rolling-window Diebold–Yılmaz (2012) connectedness framework, the paper classifies 11 crisis events between 2017 and 2025 along two orthogonal axes: the direction of the connectedness shift (integration vs. fragmentation) and the stability of the response (volatile vs. stable), with the latter benchmarked against a bootstrap-derived threshold from pre-crisis markets. The typology reveals a fragmentation paradox: supply-side shocks (armed conflicts and bilateral trade restrictions) consistently decrease market connectedness, while demand-side shocks (pandemics, monetary tightening, and financial crises) consistently increase it. This dichotomy, which is robustly preserved across all 25 event-study window specifications, challenges the prevailing assumption in the connectedness literature that crises uniformly amplify systemic risk through heightened spillovers. The mechanism is grounded in the distinction between common-factor and idiosyncratic transmission channels: supply disruptions affect individual metals asymmetrically based on their geographic exposure, fragmenting the co-movement structure, while demand shocks operate through common macroeconomic channels that drive all metals together. The typology has implications for strategic reserves policy, portfolio hedging, and energy transition risk assessment, suggesting that geopolitical risk to critical minerals supply chains is more modular than the contagion hypothesis predicts.

Global demographic change and climate policies
abstract: Between 1950 and 2017, world average life expectancy increased from below-50 to above-70, while the fertility rate dropped from 5 to about 2.5. We develop and calibrate an analytic climate-economy model with overlapping generations to study the effect of such demographic change on capital markets and optimal climate policies. Our model replicates findings from the OLG-demography literature, such as a rise in households’ savings, and a declining rate of return to capital. We also find that demographic change raises the social cost of carbon, at 2020, from 28 euro/tCO2 in a model that abstracts from demography, to 94 euro/tCO2 in our calibrated model.
